name: Overconfidence / Optimism Bias
description: People systematically overrate what they know, how well they will do, or how likely good outcomes are for them. In product work this shows up as underweighted risk, rosy self-assessments, and overconfident plans.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to self-assessment flows, privacy/security warnings, planning and estimation tools, financial or health forecasting, and any product that depends on users making realistic predictions about their own future behavior.
myth_risk_note: Unrealistic optimism is one of the most consistent psychological biases with decades of replicated evidence across health, achievement, and personal life domains, but individual-difference variation in the effect's strength keeps this from a 'none' rating.
prevalence_note: Common in behavioral-design, service-design, and product-planning discussions about risk perception and overpromising, but less universal in everyday UI-review canon than anchoring, defaults, or social proof.

findings.description: College students rated their own chances of experiencing positive future life events as above average, and negative future life events as below average, relative to their classmates (comparative/unrealistic optimism) — a bias that varied systematically with an event's desirability, perceived probability, personal experience, perceived controllability, and stereotype salience. The bias was significantly, though not fully, reduced when participants were made to consider factors that could equally affect others' chances of experiencing the same events, suggesting the bias partly stems from focusing on one's own risk-reducing factors while neglecting that others have comparable ones.
findings.source_title: Unrealistic Optimism About Future Life Events
findings.source_venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

findings.description: Overconfidence is not a single unified phenomenon but reflects three distinct, dissociable effects: overestimation of one's own actual performance, overplacement of one's performance relative to others, and overprecision (excessive certainty in one's own judgments). Overestimation and overplacement reverse direction depending on task difficulty — people overestimate their absolute performance on hard tasks but underestimate it on easy tasks, while simultaneously believing they rank worse than others on hard tasks and better than others on easy tasks (the 'hard-easy effect'). Overprecision is more persistent across difficulty levels than the other two, and its presence reduces the apparent magnitude of both overestimation and overplacement.

applications.title: Seaward & Kemp's New Zealand student-debt expectations study
applications.description: Interviewing over 200 psychology students in New Zealand about their expectations for post-graduation income, debt, and repayment timelines, researchers found students expected to pay back their student loans in an average of 10 years -- considerably faster than government statistics showed loans actually took to repay. The researchers concluded this optimism bias about future income and repayment speed likely encourages students to take on more debt than they otherwise would.
applications.industry_context: higher education finance (not a digital-product context)
applications.ethical_note: A research finding about financial self-assessment, not a persuasion or design technique -- relevant to any financial-product design context (loan calculators, repayment estimators) where a naive user-provided estimate should not be trusted at face value given this documented bias.
